title: Leaving home for Johnnie Brown's Playtone Orchestra in Mississippi
summary: Toe Morgan brings him to Jackson, Tennessee, where he joins Johnnie Brown's orchestra and tours Mississippi towns, the delta, and sees the Shiloh battlefield.

story.theme_name: Life on the road: touring bands, buses and one-nighters
story.community_name: Life on the road: buses, trains and one-nighters

blocks.x: And this same -- a buddy of mine, the fellow who got me that first job I told you about, "Toe" Morgan. His name was James "Toe" Morgan. He had a job in Jackson, Tennessee, and asked me did I want to go over to Jackson, Tennessee, and join the Johnnie Brown's orchestra. Johnnie Brown and his Playtone Orchestra.

This was a time when I told you that I left home. And my mother told me she was going to let me leave home. And that all she would ask of me was to be a good boy, and use common sense, and think of your mother while you're away. And this I did. And I joined Johnnie Brown's Playtone Orchestra. I arrived there on a Sunday, and we left Monday morning for Mississippi..

We left the Monday morning for Mississippi, on the Illinois Central. Oxford, Mississippi was where the University of Mississippi is located. This was my first town -- my first time playing in the state of Mississippi.

I can remember it was around 100 miles from Jackson because the fare back in those days was $3.00 a hundred. Our fare was $3.00 apiece. We arrived in Oxford, Mississippi. It was a quaint, old Southern city. No sidewalks. Dusty streets. They had a walkway from the station. They had a big frame walkway from the station, because there was a great big ravine or a gully in front of the station. They had a great big walkway from the station uptown about-- I guess about a block and a half. And this was a big frame walkway -- you had bannisters -- you know, you could walk up to town, see.

I remember, after we got in town. And we had a regular place. Johnnie Brown had been playing through that territory for years. We had a regular place where we would room. And I got up, and I walked around in town, looked the city over. It was just about one or two blocks. And it was no sidewalks at that time. Dusty streets. That was the summer of 1925.

We played Oxford, Mississippi. We left there and went to Water Valley -- I think it was Water Valley, and several other cities. We headed on down to Granada, Mississippi, into the delta which was Greenwood. And the delta was the most lucrative part of Mississippi so far as bands were concerned. It seemed like the people in the delta had just a little bit more money to spend than the people elsewhere. And the delta started at Greenwood, and you went through (unintelli-
on down through Indianola, down into Greenville on the Mississippi. Then you had Yazoo City. And you had other towns in Mississippi.

And so, we played those cities. We would go out and stay out maybe a week, a week and a half, then come back to Jackson. Then we'd spend a couple, two or three days. Then we would go down to Corinth, Mississippi, which was on the M&O. That was a different route, see. And going into Tupelo, Mississippi; Okolona, Mississippi; into towns like West Point, Mississippi. And, of course, Starkville, Mississippi, and Aberdeen. And then we'd come back to Tupelo, and we'd go back over west to New Albany, Mississippi.

And so, I used to keep a diary of all these cities that we played, see. And I can remember in Corinth -- we played in Corinth, and that was where the Battle of Shiloh was fought on the Tennessee River. And I made a special trip out there to see where General Johnson was shot, and the tree where he died when they laid him up against a tree where he died. And that to me, that was American history, you know, that I wanted to see with my own eyes.
